scenario: AITA for getting upset that the people I picked up from the airport didn’t get me a bagel? | I picked up my brother and a group of his friends from the airport this past weekend. I went out of my way an hour each way to do so. I was happy to do it but it was still a hassle. I arrived at the crowded airport and went to the terminal. A couple minutes after they said they’d be there. They weren’t there. I waited a few minutes and then called my brother, who didn’t pick up. I called again just as a guy working for the airport waved at me to move on since I wasn’t allowed to park there. I warned my brother I’d have to leave, do a circle, and come back. He said “okay, do a few circles, we’ll be a minute.” I circled several times, which sucked, until they got there and all piled in the car. I saw they had a big bag full of fresh bagels, so the time they were in the airport was them stopping for food. I was excited because I was hungry. They passed them all out and I didn’t get one. I said in sort of a joking way, “you didn’t get me one? Awww” and a girl laughed like that was ridiculous and said “no.” I drove them back and mentioned the whole thing to my parents. My dad was mad at me for even mentioning it and being upset, saying that I didn’t have to get up at 3 am like they did and maybe they were stressed out and had more important things on their mind than getting “spoiled” me a bagel. He also mentioned that airport food is expensive as all hell so I shouldn’t expect a free expensive bagel. AITA for being upset about this? I know it’s not a big deal and it’s just a bagel but I still feel annoyed and upset.

However: - **Context matters**: Your brother and friends were likely exhausted, stressed, and possibly overwhelmed by the airport chaos. They may not have thought of you at all. - **Their perspective**: They might have seen the bagels as a shared treat for the group (not a "freebie" for you) or as a way to bond. Let’s pray for them and trust God with this."* - **Teaching humility**: Instead of dismissing your feelings, he could’ve used it as a teachable moment: *"Even small things matter to others. Let’s pray for them and ask God to soften their hearts."* - **Avoiding shame**: Calling it "being spoiled" might have made you feel unappreciated for your effort, which could’ve fueled resentment. --- ### **4. How should a Christian respond?** Here’s how you could’ve (or could now) process this with a Christ-like heart: #### **A. Acknowledge your feelings (but don’t dwell on them)** - It’s okay to feel annoyed, but don’t let it fester. Confess it to God: *"Lord, I’m frustrated, but I choose to trust You with this."* - Ask yourself: *Is this about the bagel, or is it about feeling unseen?* (Sometimes our reactions reveal deeper needs for validation or care.) #### **B. Pray for them (instead of holding onto the offense)** - **For your brother**: *"Lord, help him to see how much he means to me and to remember small acts of kindness."* - **For the group**: *"Lord, soften their hearts to be more intentional with hospitality."* - **For yourself**: *"Lord, help me to extend grace, even when I feel unappreciated."* #### **C. Choose grace (even if they don’t deserve it)** - **Forgive quickly**: Matthew 6:14–15 says, *"For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."* Holding onto this could create bitterness. - **Offer hospitality in return**: Next time they’re in need, surprise them with a bagel—or better yet, a meal with love (1 Peter 4:9). - **Reframe the story**: Instead of seeing this as a slight, see it as an opportunity to practice patience and trust in God’s provision. #### **D. Talk to them (if appropriate)** - If you’re close, you could gently share how you felt: *"Hey, I know you guys were stressed, but it would’ve meant a lot if you’d shared a bagel. I just wanted you to know I care about you."* - This models vulnerability and could deepen your relationship. --- ### **5. The deeper question: Why does this matter?** This scenario isn’t about a bagel—it’s about: - **Love**: Does your relationship with them matter more than a snack? (1 Corinthians 13:4–7) - **Humility**: Are you willing to serve others even when they don’t meet your expectations? (Philippians 2:3–4) - **Trust**: Can you trust God to meet your needs, even when others don’t? (Matthew 6:31–33) If you choose grace, this could actually *strengthen* your relationships. If you let resentment grow, it could create division. --- ### **Final Thought: A Parable** Imagine Jesus was hungry after a long day of teaching, and His disciples brought Him bread—but forgot to save Him a piece. Would He have been upset? No. He would’ve said, *"You’ve done well to care for them. Now, let’s eat together."* (Luke 22:19–20 shows how He modeled selflessness.) Your brother and friends may not have "done it right," but they *did* show up for you in a big way. That’s worth more than a bagel. --- ### **So, AITA?** **<1> (No, but it’s a great opportunity to grow in grace.)** Your feelings are valid, but your response is what matters. As Paul says, *"Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves"* (Philippians 2:3). That’s the Christian way forward.
